notes.front: In the Cloud Digital Leader study guide, what is ‘the cloud’?
notes.back: Computing power, database storage, apps and other resources delivered over the internet on demand and paid for as they are used.
notes.explanation: Two ideas carry the definition: resources arrive when requested, through the internet, and the bill follows actual use.
notes.example: Like paying a metered electricity bill instead of running your own generator: a small firm runs its accounts software on a provider’s servers and pays only for the hours it uses.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “What is the cloud?”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is digital transformation?
notes.back: An organisation using modern digital technologies, such as cloud platforms, to create or change its business processes, culture and customer experiences.
notes.explanation: The study guide ties the change to a purpose: keeping pace with shifting business and market conditions.
notes.example: Like a high-street bank that moves account opening from paper forms at the counter to a phone app built on a cloud platform, and retrains its staff to work the new way.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “What is digital transformation?”, p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In cloud computing, what does ‘infrastructure’ refer to?
notes.back: The underlying resources that applications run on, such as compute, storage and networking, among others.
notes.explanation: Google’s comparison of service models counts virtualisation as infrastructure too, and describes a provider supplying these resources on demand through the cloud.
notes.example: Like the roads, water pipes and power lines beneath a town: the servers, disks and network links underneath an online shop’s website.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “PaaS vs. IaaS vs. SaaS vs. CaaS: How are they different?”, “IaaS”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is agentic AI?
notes.back: AI systems that can plan on their own, use tools and interact with other systems to complete complex, multistep workflows.
notes.explanation: The study guide stresses independence: the system itself plans the steps and calls on tools and other systems as it goes.
notes.example: Like a travel assistant that, told ‘book my trip to Lisbon’, compares flights, reserves a hotel through the hotel’s booking system and adds the dates to your calendar by itself.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Agentic AI”, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is open source software?
notes.back: Software whose source code is made public so that anyone can inspect, modify and enhance it.
notes.explanation: Reading the code is only part of it: the study guide’s definition also lets anyone change and improve the software.
notes.example: Like a recipe posted publicly that any cook may read, adapt and share back with their improvements.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Open standard versus open source”, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is an open standard?
notes.back: A publicly available specification for a technology, giving different systems a common language or framework.
notes.explanation: The key word is specification: the study guide means a published description of how a technology works, set beside open source software as a separate idea.
notes.example: Like standard plug and socket shapes: any manufacturer can build a kettle that fits, and no single company owns the sockets.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “Open standard versus open source”, p. 2
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Where does the term ‘integration tax’ appear in the Cloud Digital Leader study guide?
notes.back: In its list of common drivers of digital transformation: organisations transform partly to avoid integration tax.
notes.explanation: The guide names it without a definition, next to the need for a connected architecture and flexible solutions.
notes.example: The guide gives no worked case, and this deck does not guess one: treat the phrase as a label to recognise when it appears among answer options.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “What is digital transformation?” (common drivers), p. 1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework?
notes.back: Google’s recommendations for designing and operating cloud topologies that are secure, efficient, resilient, high-performing, cost-effective and sustainable.
notes.explanation: It is written for everyone who builds or runs on the cloud, not only architects: developers, administrators and other practitioners too.
notes.example: Like a building code for cloud systems: a team planning a new online store checks its design against the framework’s advice on security, cost and resilience.
notes.source: Google Cloud Architecture Center, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: The Well-Architected Framework provides recommendations to help architects, developers, administrators, and other cloud practitioners design and operate a cloud topology that's secure, efficient, resilient, high-performing, cost-effective, and sustainable.

notes.front: The study guide’s definition of the cloud describes its pricing as {{c1::pay-as-you-go}}.

notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “What is the cloud?”, p. 1

notes.front: A retailer wants extra server capacity for a two-week holiday sale, paid for only while it runs and without buying any hardware. Which part of the study guide’s definition of the cloud does this rely on?

A) Open standards shared across vendors
B) Agentic AI planning multistep workflows
C) On-demand delivery with pay-as-you-go pricing
D) Avoiding integration tax
notes.choicesExplained: A: open standards are shared specifications, not a way to obtain capacity. B: agentic AI plans and carries out tasks; it does not supply servers. D: integration tax is a driver of transformation, not part of the cloud’s definition.
notes.explanation: The guide defines the cloud as on-demand delivery of resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing, which fits a short burst of need.
notes.source: Cloud Digital Leader study guide, “Digital Transformation with Google Cloud”, “What is the cloud?”, p. 1

notes.front: Which Well-Architected Framework pillar covers deploying, operating, monitoring and managing cloud workloads efficiently?
notes.back: Operational excellence.
notes.explanation: Security, privacy and compliance is the next pillar in the list; running workloads day to day belongs to operational excellence.

notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Operational excellence Efficiently deploy, operate, monitor, and manage your cloud workloads. security Security, privacy, and compliance Maximize the security of your data and workloads in the cloud

notes.front: Which Well-Architected Framework pillar covers securing data and workloads, designing for privacy and aligning with regulatory requirements?
notes.back: Security, privacy, and compliance.
notes.explanation: Regulation sits in this pillar, not in reliability, which is about resilient and highly available workloads.
notes.source: Google Cloud Architecture Center, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Pillars”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Security, privacy, and compliance Maximize the security of your data and workloads in the cloud, design for privacy, and align with regulatory requirements and standards. restore Reliability Design and operate resilient and highly available workloads in the cloud.

notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY 4.0
notes.evidence: Reliability Design and operate resilient and highly available workloads in the cloud. payment Cost optimization Maximize the business value of your investment in Google Cloud.

notes.evidence: Cost optimization Maximize the business value of your investment in Google Cloud. speed Performance optimization Design and tune your cloud resources for optimal performance.

notes.front: Which Well-Architected Framework pillar is about designing and tuning cloud resources for optimal performance?

notes.front: In the Well-Architected Framework, what is a perspective, as opposed to a pillar?
notes.back: A cross-pillar view of recommendations for a specific technology, domain or sector.
notes.explanation: A perspective’s recommendations align with the general principles and recommendations in the pillars.
notes.source: Google Cloud Architecture Center, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Well-Architected Framework pillars and perspectives”

notes.front: A company’s architects want Google’s guidance on meeting regulators’ requirements for how customer records are stored. Which Well-Architected Framework pillar should they start from?
notes.back: B: Security, privacy, and compliance.
notes.choices:
A) Performance optimization
B) Security, privacy, and compliance
C) Operational excellence
D) Sustainability
notes.choicesExplained: A: performance optimization is about tuning resources for performance. C: operational excellence is about deploying, operating, monitoring and managing workloads. D: sustainability is about environmentally sustainable workloads.
notes.explanation: This pillar’s stated aims include designing for privacy and aligning with regulatory requirements and standards.
notes.source: Google Cloud Architecture Center, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Pillars”
